In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of the agricultural landscape in Malta in the mid-19th century, before the heavy mechanization of agriculture, which started in the 1960s and 1970s, with the introduction of the tractor and the use of chemical fertilizers.
the development of a GIS-based predictive model that can be used as an interpretative tool for the understanding of agricultural land suitability before heavy mechanisation.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Maltese landscape has been shaped through a complex interplay between natural and human factors, and the present study provides a new perspective on how this process has taken place.

the Maltese agricultural landscape, in the absence of a large-scale mechanization, was the product of a complex interplay between the topography and human mobility and accessibility, which in turn was influenced by a host of cultural factors, including the availability of land, the social and political context, and the economic and technological constraints.
the agricultural suitability of the land was a result of a complex interaction between topographic and cultural determinants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our study is a successful attempt to use historical data for modelling purposes.
the use of historical maps and GIS is very promising for the study of the agricultural history and landscape change.
the use of historical cadastral data, when available and well preserved, can be a valuable source of information to model agricultural suitability.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is feasible to model agricultural suitability using the data from 1860s cabreo.

it shows the potential of the use of historical cadastral data for the study of the determinants of agricultural suitability, a topic that is of paramount importance in the context of the present debate on the sustainability of agriculture and food security.

it provides a methodology to model land suitability in the absence of more recent and detailed data, which is often the case in the study of the historical landscapes of the Mediterranean and elsewhere.
